summary: Shafer Butte's 1926-27 cabin was replaced by a 1958 R-6 cab on a concrete base; the lookout still stands on ski-area land, used by ski patrol and for emergencies.

facts.design: 14x14-ft R-6 flattop cab on a 10-ft concrete block base (1958); sources disagree on whether a second R-6 cab was added on top in 1980

access.note: Used by the Bogus Basin ski patrol and for emergencies. The climbing guide says roads to the summit are not open to motorcycles or ATVs except government and Bogus Basin vehicles. No public visiting is described in these sources.

visit.trail_note: The summit sits inside the Bogus Basin ski area. Roads and cat tracks lead toward the summit, and the climbing guide describes summer hiking and biking there. The cab itself is not described as open to visitors.

facts.agency: U.S. Forest Service, Boise National Forest (per NHLR); the climbing guide says the Forest Service no longer uses the lookout

events.note: First lookout: two-story cabin set up by the Southern Idaho Timber Protective Association (NHLR). Firelookout.com gives 1927 as the year it was first used.
August 14, 1926 newspaper item (as quoted by Forest Lookouts) reports a fire from the Shafer Butte lookout station.
Late-summer 1926 electrical-storm fires in the Boise basin; the lookout station reported one with a three-mile front.
Official opening of the lookout station (September 28, 1928 item), attended by Senator William E. Borah and the U.S. chief forester.

June 29, 1929: forest office reports the road to the lookout is now negotiable for automobiles. September 27, 1929: with fire danger over, lookouts and crews are taken out, but lookouts will be kept on the butte for emergency purposes.

October 6, 1936 item: a 1495-pound periscope borrowed from the United States navy for experimental purposes was used on Shafer Butte for the first time in actual fire detection; results reported as highly satisfactory.
Mrs. Lucy Schlosman on lookout duty (January 28, 1945 item); she looked after weather instruments and called in readings four times a day.
July 25, 1948 item: the Standleys used the lower portion of the lookout as a kitchen and a general living and dining room.
Boise National Forest replaced the cabin with a 14x14-ft R-6 flattop cab on a 10-ft concrete block base. NHLR gives 1958 as the build date.
Mrs. Ronald Ashley, observer at the Shaffer Lookout, early July 1959 (item dated July 2, 1959).
Stan Boyd listed as known staff.

Second R-6 cab placed on top of the first, or a three-story structure erected in place of the two-story one; the 1980 date comes from Forest Lookouts and Idaho Fire Lookouts. The register describes three floors without dating the change.
Original viewing platform removed from the summit and a new communications tower added.
Climbing guide (updated February 2021): still standing but no longer used by the Forest Service.

corrections.proposed: remove (no current height in any source read)
corrections.why: No source read gives a 3 m height for the lookout. The 1959 NGS description of the earlier two-story house says it was 30 feet high, and no source gives the current height.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register says 1926 and firelookout.com says 1927. An August 1926 newspaper item already reports a fire from the lookout station, which supports 1926. The story uses 1926 and notes the 1927 date.

The register describes three floors after the 1958 cab: a ground floor that was living quarters long ago and later a radio and storage room, a second floor that became living quarters, and a third floor used for the alidade and observation. Forest Lookouts and Idaho Fire Lookouts date a three-story or second R-6 cab to 1980, and firelookout.com gives no date. The story reports both views.

The register gives 7,502 ft (2,287 m), which matches the record's elevation_m. The climbing guide and firelookout.com give 7,582 ft. The difference may be a transposed digit. The story reports both figures.

notes_for_editor: Read the NHLR page, the Forest Lookouts page (including its 1926-1959 newspaper extracts and its 1959 NGS survey description), Idaho Fire Lookouts, the climbing guide (updated Feb 2021) and firelookout.com. One WebSearch-equivalent search was run; the Idaho Statesman article it surfaced timed out twice and is not used. Access is recorded as restricted because the sources describe ski patrol occupancy and emergency use with no public visiting, but no source states the access rule outright, so a human should confirm before publishing. The 1980 change to the upper floors is disputed. The brief's height_m of 3.0 has no support in any source read and is proposed for removal. The brief's elevation_m (2286.6) matches NHLR's 7,502 ft, but three other sources give 7,582 ft. Fact-check 2026-10-08: every dated item in the story was confirmed on the cached Forest Lookouts page and the NHLR register text; the story's floor wording now follows the register, and the 'Please do not climb the tower' line is safety advice, not a sourced fact.
